resources.string: What is it for?
your code
processor
You write total equals price plus two. The processor does not understand that: it only runs simple instructions.
Which of the two does the processor understand? Tap it.
It only reads short instructions, like load, add and store.
Machine code. The compiler is the program that translates your code into that.
Translating everything in one go would be hard to do and to check. So the work is split up.
The compiler works in six phases, one after another. What comes out of one phase is the input of the next.
The analysis ends with intermediate code. It writes one operation per line, independent of the machine.
From here on it's the synthesis. Optimization improves that code without changing the result. Code generation writes the final machine code.
What comes out of each phase
The recipe is what comes out of each phase. Remember the order, because exams ask for it.
Lexical → tokens
Syntactic → tree
Semantic → tree with types
Intermediate → one operation per line
Optimization → fewer operations
Generation → machine code
Each phase catches one kind of error. A character that forms no token is a lexical error. A token out of order is a syntax error.
A well-formed sentence with no meaning, such as a wrong type or an undeclared variable, is a semantic error.
Another piece of code
Now this while goes through the same phases.
Who cuts the while into tokens? Tap the phase.
It's the first phase. It only looks at the letters.
The lexical phase cuts and names each piece.
If the closing parenthesis is missing, which phase complains?
The letters are fine. What's missing is the shape of the statement.
A parenthesis without its pair breaks the tree. That's syntactic.
In which phase does the loop turn into jumps, one operation per line?
It comes after the semantic phase and before optimization.
Exactly. Intermediate code writes the loop with jumps.
Six phases in order. The analysis goes up to the intermediate code, and the synthesis starts from it. The game map follows that same path.
The parser has T on top of the stack and reads id. T has two rules, and it may look at one token only.
With id in the input, which of the two rules works? Tap it.
One rule starts with an open paren. The token read is id.
T goes to id. You could tell because that rule starts with the token itself.
To choose without backtracking, it must know which token each rule can start with.
FIRST of a symbol is the set of terminals that can appear at the start of what it generates.
Let's compute it for this grammar. Each nonterminal gets a bag, and its FIRST fills up bit by bit.
FIRST recipe
The FIRST recipe has four steps. You apply them to every rule of the grammar.
1. Starts with a terminal: it goes in.
2. Starts with a nonterminal: its FIRST, minus ε.
3. If it is nullable, look at the next symbol.
Step one: the rule starts with a terminal. It goes into FIRST, and that rule is done.
For E goes to T X, which step of the recipe do you use? Tap it.
E starts with T, and T is a nonterminal with rules of its own.
Nice. Step two: FIRST of T goes into FIRST of E, minus epsilon.
Step three: if that nonterminal is nullable, it can vanish. So the next symbol can also start the rule.
Another grammar. Now you do the computing. Start with A, because S depends on it.
A has two rules: a followed by A, and epsilon. Tap what goes into FIRST of A.
One rule starts with the terminal a. The other is epsilon.
The a goes in by step one. Epsilon goes in because A is nullable.
S goes to A b. The a from A already goes into FIRST of S. But A is nullable. Which other token can start S?
If A vanishes, b is left at the start.
By step three, b goes in. The epsilon from A stays out, because b never vanishes.
The other rule of S is left. Tap what goes in through it.
The second rule of S starts with a terminal.
You got it. The letter c goes in by step one.
FIRST of S: a, b and c. One more round changes nothing, so the computation is over.
One more exam case. Notice: the rule of B has no epsilon written in it.
Even so, can B vanish? Tap the answer.
Follow B goes to C. What can C become?
It can. B goes to C, and C goes to epsilon. So FIRST of B has b, c and epsilon.
Now S goes to B d. Tap everything that goes into FIRST of S.
Use FIRST of B without the epsilon. And since B vanishes, look at the next one.
Three tokens: b, c and d. The d goes in because B vanishes. The epsilon stays out, because d never vanishes.
In rule order, the first round leaves S with only the d. That's because B is still empty. The next rounds bring the b and the c. That's why step four says to repeat.
The parser has X on top and reads close paren. X is nullable: it can vanish, or it can become plus T X.
No rule of X starts with a close paren. Which one does the parser use? Tap it.
One of the rules lets X vanish.
X goes to epsilon. X vanishes, and the close paren is left for what comes next.
Vanishing is only right if close paren can appear right after X. FIRST cannot answer that.
FOLLOW of a nonterminal is the set of terminals that can appear right after it in some derivation.
Same grammar, three bags again. Now each bag holds what can come after the nonterminal.
FOLLOW recipe
The FOLLOW recipe has four steps. For each nonterminal B, find where it appears on a right-hand side.
1. End of input: the start symbol gets $.
2. After B: FIRST, minus ε. Vanishes? Next one.
3. End of rule: inherit FOLLOW of the left side.
Step one: the start symbol gets the dollar sign, which marks the end of input.
Plus, which is in FIRST of X, went into FOLLOW of T. Which step did that? Tap.
X comes right after T. It's the FIRST of what comes after.
That's it. Step two: FIRST of what comes after, minus epsilon.
Step three: if everything after B can vanish, or nothing comes after it, you reached the end of the rule. Then B inherits FOLLOW of whoever is left of the arrow.
Now a bigger grammar, with addition and multiplication. The goal is FOLLOW of F.
In T goes to F Y, Y comes after F. Which token can Y start with? Tap.
Look at the rules of Y. One of them starts with a terminal.
Times goes in by step two.
Y is nullable. So F can end up last in the rule of T. Whose FOLLOW does F inherit? Tap.
F is on the right-hand side of the rule of T.
By step three, everything that follows T also follows F.
FOLLOW of T has plus, close paren and dollar. All three go into FOLLOW of F.
FOLLOW of F: times, plus, close paren and dollar. Another round changes nothing.
Now the case that trips people up most on exams. Two symbols come after B: C and d.
C can vanish. Tap everything that goes into FOLLOW of B.
C can become c. And if C vanishes, what comes right after B?
Two tokens. The c comes from FIRST of C. Since C vanishes, the d goes in too.
That's the end of step two: if the neighbor vanishes, look at the next one. Stopping at C forgets the d.
